summary: This document extends in-band signaling of Multipoint LDP (mLDP) so one message can cover many IP multicast trees using wildcards. This helps convert multicast trees into MPLS point-to-multipoint paths when they enter an MPLS domain, and back again at the edge.

eli5.summary: Instead of announcing each TV channel to the network one at a time, you can say all channels at once. That saves a lot of messages.

questions: what does a wildcard mean in mldp
how do you attach an asm shared tree to an mpls lsp
what is threshold infinity in pim
subtitle: Lets one mLDP message cover a whole shared multicast tree, or many source trees at once, by using zeroes as a wildcard.

tldr.problem: Earlier mLDP in-band signaling could attach only one source-specific IP multicast tree, an (S,G), to each MPLS multipoint LSP, and could not attach a non-bidirectional Any-Source Multicast shared tree at all.
tldr.mechanism: A value of all zeroes in the IP source address or IP group address subfield of the mLDP Opaque Value TLV now means a wildcard, so one MP-LSP can carry a shared (*,G) tree or all the trees that share a source or a group.
tldr.outcome: Fewer MP-LSPs are needed, which saves state in the network, but the wildcard source with an ASM group is limited to cases where no source discovery or source pruning is needed. The RFC updates RFC 6826 and RFC 7246.

facts.label: TLVs extended
facts.value: Transit IPv4, IPv6, VPNv4 and VPNv6 Source TLVs

today: RFC 7438 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 6826 and RFC 7246.

sections.title: Why Wildcards Are Needed
sections.content:
Sometimes an IP multicast tree has to cross an MPLS domain. mLDP in-band signaling, defined in RFC 6826 and RFC 7246, lets the tree be attached to an MPLS multipoint LSP (MP-LSP) when it enters the domain and turned back into an IP multicast tree when it leaves. The MP-LSP is identified by a root node (the Ingress LSR) and an Opaque Value. In-band signaling puts the IP multicast tree identifier into that Opaque Value, so no other protocol is needed to bind the tree to the LSP.

The earlier documents encode one source address (S) and one group address (G), so one MP-LSP can carry only a single (S,G) tree. They also do not support attaching an Any-Source Multicast (ASM) shared tree, except a bidirectional one. This RFC fixes both gaps by letting S, G, or both be replaced by a wildcard, written as an asterisk. Aggregating several trees onto fewer MP-LSPs saves state in the network.

The RFC specifies only what is specific to wildcards. The other in-band signaling procedures of RFC 6826 and RFC 7246 still apply.
sections.eli5: Before, you had to ask for one TV show at a time. Now you can ask for every show from one studio, or a whole channel, in one go.

sections.title: Encoding and Meaning of the Wildcards
sections.content:
RFC 6826 and RFC 7246 define the Transit IPv4 Source, Transit IPv6 Source, Transit VPNv4 Source and Transit VPNv6 Source TLVs. Each has a subfield for an IP source address and one for an IP group address. This RFC allows either one, or both, to hold a wildcard instead of a valid address. The wildcard is a value of all zeroes in the subfield, and the subfield lengths stay as they were.

The meaning depends on the combination:

  • Wildcard source with an ASM group address (not in the SSM range): a PIM-SM shared tree.
  • Wildcard source with a group address in the SSM range: the collection of PIM trees with that group address.
  • Non-zero source with a wildcard group: the collection of PIM-SSM trees rooted at that source.

The structure of the Opaque Value does not affect how mLDP itself works. Only the IP multicast modules at the Ingress and Egress LSRs interpret it. A wildcard group in the Bidir TLVs, and a wildcard source together with a wildcard group in one TLV, are out of scope.
sections.eli5: A row of zeroes is a blank that means 'any'. Leave the studio blank and you get every studio; leave the channel blank and you get every channel from one studio.

sections.title: Compatibility and Limits
sections.content:
The procedures do not change the behavior of RFC 6826 and RFC 7246. An Egress LSR that does not know about wildcards never generates them. An Ingress LSR that does not support this RFC has no choice but to treat FEC elements with zeroes in those subfields as invalid. For that reason an Egress LSR MUST NOT use wildcard encodings for a given MP-LSP unless it is known in advance that the Ingress LSR supports this RFC. How that is known is outside the scope of the RFC.

There is a second limit for ASM. Supporting non-bidirectional PIM-ASM trees in general needs source discovery and source pruning, and this RFC specifies neither. So a wildcard source with an ASM group address MUST NOT be used unless it is known in advance that neither is needed. Where they are needed, in-band signaling is NOT RECOMMENDED and procedures such as those in RFC 6513 are the alternative.
sections.eli5: Both ends have to understand the blank-means-any trick, or the far end will think the message is broken. Also, it only works when you do not need to hunt for new studios or block one.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC gives three example scenarios and says the list is not exhaustive.

PIM shared tree forwarding with threshold infinity. In PIM, receivers join the shared (*,G) tree toward the Rendezvous Point (RP) and may later switch to a source tree. With threshold infinity, a last hop router keeps receiving everything on the (*,G) tree. This is often used when the shortest path from any source to any receiver goes through the RP anyway. The Egress LSRs then use a wildcard in the source subfield and G in the group subfield. PIM-ASM without threshold infinity is not supported by these procedures.

IGMP/MLD proxying. Senders and receivers attach directly to the MPLS domain and see it as a single hop, following RFC 4605. The mLDP root is manually configured, and since the MP-LSP carries all sources for the group, the source subfield is a wildcard.

Selective source mapping. In IPTV deployments with content servers gathered at a few sites, popular channels are often statically configured and forwarded over the core. They MAY be forwarded over a multipoint LSP with wildcard encoding, and the Ingress LSR selects from the streams it has state for.
sections.eli5: Think of a school where every classroom always gets the same set of morning announcements. It is simpler to set up one loudspeaker line for everything than one wire per announcement.

sections.title: Ingress and Egress Procedures
sections.content:
The IP multicast component of an Egress LSR decides, from provisioned policy, whether to use in-band signaling and whether to use a wildcard. The RFC does not make any particular policy mandatory. Its two examples: for a non-bidirectional ASM group G with the RP reachable by a BGP route, the Egress LSR may pick the BGP next hop toward the RP as the root and signal (*,G); and for a group with only an IGMP/MLD report and no PIM, it uses the proxy device as the root.

When the Ingress LSR gets a TLV with a wildcard source, it passes the subfields to its IP multicast component, which MUST follow these rules:

  1. PIM enabled and a non-bidirectional ASM group: act as if a (*,G) IGMP/MLD report arrived from downstream and follow RFC 4601.
  2. PIM enabled and a PIM-SSM group: forward all multicast sources known for the group down the MP-LSP. How the Ingress LSR receives that traffic is out of scope.
  3. PIM not enabled for the group: act as if a (*,G) report arrived and follow RFC 4605, forwarding the (*,G) packets through the MP-LSP.

For a wildcard group, the Ingress LSR looks in its multicast routing table for all streams from the source in the TLV. These streams SHOULD all be forwarded down the identified MP-LSP, whether their group addresses are SSM or ASM.
sections.eli5: The router at the sending end checks which kind of request came in and then sends down the pipe everything that matches: one channel, one studio, or all of them.

sections.title: Finding the Root and Anycast RP
sections.content:
An Egress LSR must work out which node is the root of the MP-LSP. RFC 6826 and RFC 7246 do this from the address of the multicast source S. For a (*,G) set of streams there is no single source, so the only difference is that the proxy device or RP address is used in place of the source to find the mLDP root. Other ways of choosing the root are allowed by policy.

In deployments using mLDP in-band signaling, RP-to-group mappings are unlikely to be distributed dynamically over the MPLS core. The RP address is more likely statically configured at each multicast site. The RFC advises configuring an Anycast RP address at each site for redundancy, and points to RFC 3446.
sections.eli5: When you do not know which studio sends a show, you ask the front desk, the rendezvous point, who will know where to send your request. Having a backup front desk means it still works if one is away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says there are no security considerations other than the ones already given in RFC 5036, RFC 6826 and RFC 7246. Wildcards add no new security mechanism.
sections.eli5: Using the blank-means-any trick adds no new locks or keys beyond what the older rules already use.

cells: All PIM trees with that group address
All PIM-SSM trees rooted at that source

items.title: Ingress LSR must support it
items.text: An Egress LSR MUST NOT use wildcards unless it is known in advance that the Ingress LSR supports this RFC.

items.title: ASM needs no discovery or pruning
items.text: A wildcard source with an ASM group MUST NOT be used unless source discovery and source pruning are not needed.
